summary: Describes methods for transporting layer 2 PDUs such as Frame Relay, ATM AAL5, and Ethernet across an MPLS network, and for providing SONET circuit emulation. It documents the draft-martini protocol, since superseded by pseudowire specifications such as RFC 4447. It is historic.

eli5.summary: Different kinds of network traffic can ride through one shared highway. This note describes an old way of doing it, which newer rules have replaced.

questions: what is draft-martini transport of layer 2 over mpls
how to carry ethernet over mpls
how to transport layer 2 over mpls
what is the difference between tunnel label and vc label
subtitle: An old way to carry different network protocols through one MPLS tunnel

tldr.problem: Network operators need to send various layer 2 protocols (like Frame Relay, ATM, and Ethernet) across MPLS backbone networks that normally carry IP traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The draft-martini protocol uses a two-label stack: a tunnel label for routing through the MPLS network and a virtual circuit (VC) label to identify which specific connection the data belongs to. This allows many layer 2 services to share a single tunnel.
tldr.outcome: This design was widely deployed but has been superseded by the Pseudowire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3) specifications (RFC 4447 and related RFCs), which are the modern standard for this function. RFC 4906 is now Historic and should not be used for new implementations.

today: RFC 4906 is Historic and has been superseded by the PWE3 standards, particularly RFC 4447. The draft-martini protocol is still used in some deployed networks but must not be used for new implementations.

sections.title: Carrying Layer 2 Over MPLS
sections.content:
RFC 4906 describes the draft-martini protocol, a method for transporting layer 2 protocols (such as Frame Relay, ATM, and Ethernet) across MPLS networks. MPLS networks normally carry IP packets, but this protocol makes it possible for them to also carry layer 2 frames from many different protocols.

The document covers several protocol types: Frame Relay, ATM in multiple modes, Ethernet (with or without VLAN tags), HDLC, and PPP. It also describes circuit emulation for time-division multiplexed (TDM) signals, including SONET and SDH. The protocol uses LDP (Label Distribution Protocol) to distribute labels that identify which virtual circuit each frame belongs to.
sections.eli5: This RFC shows how to take different kinds of network traffic (old phone lines, ATM networks, Ethernet) and send them through an MPLS network by wrapping each one and labeling it carefully so it gets to the right place.

sections.title: Two Labels: Tunnel and Virtual Circuit
sections.content:
The protocol uses two labels stacked on top of each frame. The tunnel label acts like a shipping address: it tells the MPLS network how to route the packet from the entry router (R1) to the exit router (R2). The virtual circuit (VC) label, which sits below the tunnel label in the stack, identifies which specific connection the data belongs to when it arrives at R2.

This two-label approach is efficient because many different virtual circuits can share a single tunnel through the backbone. The tunnel label can be distributed using any standard MPLS label distribution method. The VC label is distributed using LDP in downstream unsolicited mode, which means the egress router tells the ingress router which VC labels to use.
sections.eli5: Think of it like mail: the tunnel label is like the town name (how to route the truck), and the VC label is like the house number (which mailbox it goes to).

sections.title: Supported Protocols
sections.content:
The protocol supports several layer 2 encapsulations. Frame Relay frames are wrapped and transported using their DLCI (Data Link Connection Identifier) to identify the connection. ATM is supported in multiple modes: AAL5 (Asynchronous Transfer Mode Adaptation Layer 5) for higher-level data, transparent cell transport for individual ATM cells, and VCC/VPC cell transport for virtual channels and virtual paths. The protocol can also handle OAM (Operations and Management) cells for monitoring ATM connections.

Ethernet frames can be transported with VLAN tags intact or without them. HDLC (High-Level Data Link Control) and PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) are also supported for legacy link protocols. Each protocol type has its own VC Type code so the egress router knows how to handle the frame when it arrives.
sections.eli5: The protocol can handle old Frame Relay networks, ATM phone networks, regular Ethernet cables, old serial lines, and dial-up protocols. Each type gets its own type code so the receiver knows what to do with it.

sections.title: Control Word and Signaling
sections.content:
Some VC types require a control word, which is an extra header added after the VC label to provide sequence numbers and other information. Some VC types have the control word optional, and both endpoints must negotiate whether to use it.

The protocol defines two LDP status codes for control word issues: Illegal C-Bit (0x20000001) when a control word is required but not signaled, and Wrong C-Bit (0x20000002) when endpoints disagree about whether to use it. The Group ID field allows operators to perform wildcard withdrawals: withdrawing all VC labels associated with a group at once, which is useful when a physical port fails.
sections.eli5: Think of the control word as a tracking number on a package: some types always need it, others don't. If the sender and receiver disagree about whether to include it, they have to negotiate to find a compromise.

sections.title: Status and Historical Context
sections.content: The document explicitly states that the draft-martini protocol and its procedures have been superseded by the Pseudowire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3) working group specifications, particularly RFC 4447 (PWE3 setup using LDP) and related RFCs including RFC 4385, RFC 4448, RFC 4717, RFC 4618, RFC 4619, RFC 4553, and RFC 4842. Although draft-martini is used in many deployed implementations, new implementations must use RFC 4447 and the PWE3 specifications instead. RFC 4906 serves as documentation of existing implementations only.
sections.eli5: This old method still works in many networks, but there is a newer, better way called PWE3 that replaced it. If you are building something new, use the newer way instead.
